MI-Q001: Resolution distinguishes neighbouring points as separate. Magnification enlarges an image, contrast makes structures differ from their background, and depth of field concerns the range appearing sharp. Increasing one does not automatically improve the others. A large, visible blur can therefore still fail to resolve two structures.
MI-Q002: The simple microscope uses a converging magnifying lens to create the enlarged apparent image. A compound microscope uses distinct objective/eyepiece systems; an electron beam belongs to a different imaging method. Some modern loupes have several lens elements, so compact appearance alone does not prove a strictly single-lens design.
MI-Q003: Chromatic aberration follows wavelength-dependent refraction: different colours focus differently. Spherical aberration instead concerns rays at different distances from the lens axis. Condenser alignment and numerical aperture can affect image quality without being the cause of that colour-dependent focusing defect. Diagnose the optical mechanism rather than treating every blur as the same problem.
MI-Q004: The objective first forms the magnified intermediate image that the eyepiece enlarges further. The eyepiece is therefore not interchangeable with the specimen-side objective. A compound light microscope does not project an electron image. This two-stage arrangement explains why their magnifications multiply for the usual total-magnification calculation.
MI-Q005: Parfocal objectives keep the specimen approximately focused when the selected objective changes, reducing the adjustment required. Approximately matters: minor focusing may still be needed. Parfocality does not mean constant magnification or working distance, and it cannot justify forcing a high-power objective into the slide.
MI-Q006: Numerical aperture describes the range of image-forming light collected and depends on refractive index and acceptance angle. In the stated relationship r=0.61λ/NA, larger NA reduces the minimum resolvable distance at fixed wavelength. Eyepiece enlargement alone does not supply that optical information; practical resolution also depends on the specimen and setup.
MI-Q007: Dark-field excludes direct illumination from the objective while allowing specimen-scattered light to enter. The specimen can therefore appear bright against a dark background without emitting fluorescence. Letting direct rays form a bright field would change the illumination mechanism. Improved visibility should not be confused with automatically improving the diffraction-limited resolving distance.
MI-Q008: Transparent living structures may change optical phase while absorbing little light. Phase-contrast optics convert those differences into intensity contrast, allowing observation without conventional fixation/staining. Metal-coated specimens and electron transmission belong to electron microscopy. Better contrast does not remove the resolving limit imposed by the visible-light optical system.
MI-Q009: Shorter wavelength can reduce the diffraction-limited resolving distance when other optical conditions are suitable. Larger eyepiece magnification only enlarges the image; specimen thickness does not explain the wavelength advantage. A longer wavelength tends in the opposite direction. UV requires suitable optics and protective detection arrangements, not direct unprotected viewing.
MI-Q010: An antibody supplies target recognition and a direct or indirect fluorescent label supplies the detectable signal. Untargeted fluorescent lipids do not by themselves identify the intended antigen. Heavy-metal contrast and silver-halide tracer detection are different signal mechanisms. Specificity still requires suitable controls rather than interpreting any bright spot as proof of the target.
MI-Q011: TEM uses electrons transmitted through appropriately thin specimens to reveal internal ultrastructure. SEM emphasizes surface-related signals; fluorescence localizes labels by emitted light. A conventional prepared TEM specimen is not simply a living cell viewed in air. Thinness, preservation and electron contrast all affect what can be interpreted.
MI-Q012: SEM scans a surface and detects signals that reveal morphology/topography. It is distinct from TEM transmission through ultrathin sections and from light-based live-cell or fluorescent imaging. A large depth of field can produce a three-dimensional appearance, but one conventional SEM image is not automatically a complete quantitative 3D reconstruction.
MI-Q013: Preparation addresses preservation, support, thickness and contrast so the specimen is compatible with the imaging method. It does not increase the objective's numerical aperture, equalize every organelle's density or eliminate biological variability. Each stage solves a different problem; an ultrathin but poorly preserved specimen can still produce misleading structural evidence.
MI-Q014: Fixation stabilises cellular constituents and limits autolysis and post-collection deterioration. Dehydration removes water for later processing, and staining supplies contrast; they are not synonyms for fixation. Removing every lipid would destroy rather than preserve some structures. The appropriate fixative and conditions depend on the specimen and intended analysis.
MI-Q015: Dehydration removes tissue water, commonly through graded alcohols. Clearing then replaces alcohol with a medium compatible with the embedding workflow, and infiltration supplies support. It does not primarily remove wax, heavy-metal stains or every nucleic acid. Explain the sequence of replacements rather than memorising one reagent name without its role.
MI-Q016: A microtome cuts sections of controlled thickness using a specimen holder, cutting edge and thickness mechanism. Electron-beam generation, absorbance measurement and condenser illumination are different instrument functions. The support medium and cutting edge must suit the sectioning task; ultrathin TEM preparation has different requirements from routine wax sections.
MI-Q017: Routine H&E commonly gives blue-purple nuclear staining from the haematoxylin staining complex, while eosin gives many protein-rich regions pink-red. The contrast depends on staining chemistry and preparation, not merely a nucleus having a particular pH. A colour pattern supports structural interpretation but is not unique molecular identification.
MI-Q018: Negative stain produces a relatively electron-dense background around the particle, making the specimen comparatively light. Selectively darkening specimen structures instead describes positive staining. The specimen holder or vacuum is not the intended contrasting region. Ask where the heavy material lies before interpreting a bright outline against a dark field.
OR01-Q01: The lecturer's microbodies have a single limiting membrane that separates their specialised reactions from surrounding cytoplasm. This differs from a double-membrane organelle or a membrane-less region. Membrane count helps classify structure but does not make all microbodies metabolically interchangeable; their enzyme systems and functions differ.
OR01-Q02: Catalase removes peroxide through reactions including 2H₂O₂→2H₂O+O₂. Peroxisomal oxidases can generate peroxide, so production and removal are coordinated but distinct roles. An enzyme involved in another substrate's oxidation is not automatically the peroxide-removing enzyme. Compartmentalisation helps manage reactive products without implying that peroxide never forms normally.
OR01-Q03: Humans lack functional urate oxidase, despite the lecturer's cross-organism list of peroxisomal enzymes. That species qualification does not mean humans lack peroxisomes or catalase. The human urate-oxidase gene's nonfunctional status has independent molecular evidence. Keep organism, enzyme and metabolic step separate when applying a general organelle description to human physiology.
OR01-Q04: Peroxisomes participate in oxidative metabolism, including fatty-acid breakdown. Their peroxide-producing and peroxide-removing enzymes help manage that chemistry. This differs from lysosomal acid hydrolysis or nuclear information processing. Naming one associated process does not imply that the organelle is the exclusive location of every fatty-acid or detoxification pathway.
OR01-Q05: Hydrogen peroxide can oxidatively damage cellular molecules if it accumulates, so its removal by catalase is important. Peroxide production can nevertheless be a normal product of oxidative reactions rather than proof of malfunction. The cross-organism uricase example needs its human qualification; humans lack functional uricase but still require peroxisomal peroxide management.
OR03-Q01: The H⁺-ATPase uses ATP to move protons into the lumen, maintaining conditions favourable for acid hydrolases. The pump establishes acidity rather than directly digesting every substrate. DNA helicase, ribosomal subunits and centriole structures have different roles. Compartment conditions and the enzymes acting within them are related but distinct requirements.
OR03-Q02: The source gives an approximate lysosomal pH of 5.0, maintained by inward proton pumping. It is acidic compared with neutral or near-neutral values such as 7.4, but the lecturer does not specify pH 2.0 here. This is a representative lumen condition rather than a universal constant for every compartment at every stage.
OR03-Q03: Autophagy delivers a cell's own components for lysosomal degradation and recycling. Heterophagy concerns material originating outside the cell. Transcription produces RNA and glycolysis is a metabolic pathway, not the corresponding cargo-delivery distinction. Regulated autophagy in a living cell is also different from autolysis after tissue deterioration or death.
OR03-Q04: Phagocytosis encloses engulfed material in a phagosome, which can subsequently interact with lysosomal compartments. A nucleosome packages DNA, a centrosome organises microtubules and a peroxisome carries out specialised metabolism. The compartment's origin and cargo matter: a vesicle containing engulfed material is not identified solely by being membrane-bound.
OR03-Q05: A residual body retains material that has not been completely digested. It is not a site of rRNA transcription, a membrane-less DNA region or a centriole precursor. Lysosomal enzyme content does not guarantee that every substrate is degradable. Remaining material may persist or be expelled depending on the cell and context.
OR04-Q01: Persistent injury and inflammation can promote fibroblast activity and collagen deposition, producing fibrosis and impaired lung mechanics. Nuclear pores, ribosomal assembly and the glyoxylate cycle do not explain that tissue-scarring chain. The source compares dust-related diseases, but silica, asbestos and coal-dust exposure are not interchangeable diagnoses or identical mechanisms.
OR04-Q02: β-Hexosaminidase A participates in GM2 degradation; deficient activity in Tay–Sachs permits substrate accumulation. Catalase concerns peroxide removal, urate oxidase concerns urate metabolism in organisms possessing it, and DNA polymerase concerns DNA synthesis. Identify the blocked reaction rather than assume any missing cellular enzyme would cause the same storage disorder.
OR04-Q03: GM2 ganglioside accumulates when its lysosomal degradation is impaired by deficient β-hexosaminidase A activity. It is a lipid substrate, not succinate, peroxide or collagen. Those distractors belong to different pathways or tissue responses. Selective substrate accumulation illustrates enzyme specificity and helps explain why one lysosomal defect can especially affect particular cells.
OR04-Q04: Tay–Sachs can occur in people of any ancestry, although carrier frequencies are higher in some populations. Nationality itself is not the cause, and an ancestry association cannot exclude the disease elsewhere. Molecular variants and enzyme function underlie the disorder; this learning question does not replace clinical testing or individual risk assessment.
OR04-Q05: Deficiency of a particular lysosomal enzyme can prevent degradation of its usual substrate, causing accumulation. It does not inherently duplicate chromosomes, add nuclear pores or remove centrioles. Other lysosomal enzymes may still function, so the consequence is not necessarily total loss of intracellular digestion. Follow the missing reaction and its substrate to understand the mechanism.
CM_MCQ_24-90: Lateral diffusion occurs within the plane of a leaflet. Flip-flop transfers a lipid between leaflets and requires a different movement through the membrane's core. The fluid bilayer can remain an effective barrier while constituents move within it. Movement alone does not mean the membrane has dissolved or that every molecule changes sides freely.
CM_MCQ_24-91: Cis-unsaturated tails contain bends that interfere with close packing compared with straighter saturated chains under otherwise similar conditions. This affects membrane fluidity rather than making the polar head disappear. Temperature and other composition also matter, so the comparison should not be turned into an unconditional claim about every membrane.
CM_MCQ_24-92: At relatively low temperatures, cholesterol interferes with close phospholipid packing and can help avoid abrupt solidification. At warmer temperatures it can restrain excessive movement. The effects are conditional rather than contradictory: cholesterol buffers physical behaviour. It neither always increases fluidity nor eliminates all lipid movement in every condition.
CM_MCQ_24-93: Spontaneous flip-flop is relatively rare because the polar head must pass through the unfavourable nonpolar core. Lateral movement stays within a leaflet and is comparatively easier. Enzymes can facilitate transbilayer movement, so rare spontaneous movement is not the same as impossible transfer. The source's rates are illustrations, not universal fixed frequencies.
CM_MCQ_24-94: Cooling generally reduces molecular motion and can favour more ordered packing, with the transition depending on lipid composition. Unsaturated tails and cholesterol modify that behaviour, so temperature is not the only determinant. A change in fluidity concerns membrane physical properties; it does not mean that all membrane components vanish or stop functioning identically.
CM_MCQ_24-95: At relatively high temperatures, cholesterol can restrain excessive phospholipid mobility. This complements its disruption of close packing during cooling. The answer therefore depends on the stated temperature condition and does not mean complete arrest of diffusion. Compare physical packing and movement instead of treating cholesterol as a one-direction fluidity switch.
CM_MCQ_24-102: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, making passage through the lipid core relatively favourable. Charged ions and many polar substances face different barriers and often require transport proteins for efficient movement. Selective permeability is not a rule that everything small crosses equally quickly. The actual rate still depends on the molecule and membrane conditions.
CM_MCQ_24-103: For an ion, concentration and electrical potential jointly contribute to the electrochemical gradient. Their effects may reinforce or oppose each other. Concentration alone therefore cannot always predict net passive direction, and a driving force does not establish that a suitable membrane pathway exists. Permeability and energetic tendency are different parts of the explanation.
CM_MCQ_24-104: Aquaporins provide pathways that greatly increase water permeability in many membranes. Water can also cross a lipid bilayer to some extent, so the channel is not proof of an absolute inability to cross otherwise. A water channel is not automatically a pump or a transport route for every ion and large cargo.
CM_MCQ_24-105: Vesicular transport moves large cargo through membrane-enclosed uptake or release processes such as endocytosis and exocytosis. That differs from individual molecules diffusing through the lipid core or a channel. A large object does not become bilayer-permeable merely because it has a concentration gradient. Match cargo scale with the transport mechanism.
CM_MCQ_24-106: The lecture's representative animal-cell pattern has higher K⁺ inside and higher Na⁺ outside. Maintaining such distributions requires regulated transport; it is not proof that every ion moves inward passively. The electrical gradient also matters to an ion's net tendency. These examples do not establish identical concentrations in every cell or physiological condition.
CM_MCQ_24-107: Membrane potential is an electrical voltage difference across the membrane. It is distinct from a concentration difference, although both influence ions through an electrochemical gradient. It does not mean that all fluid on one side carries a uniform massive net charge. Interpret voltage, concentration and permeability separately before predicting transport.
CYQ13: The centrosome is a major microtubule-organising centre in many animal cells. Its pericentriolar material helps nucleate and organise microtubules, rather than serving lysosomal digestion or nucleolar rRNA assembly. Not every eukaryote has a canonical centrosome, so the cellular context is important to the answer.
CYQ14: Tau is a microtubule-associated protein whose abnormal behaviour is implicated in Alzheimer pathology. Myosin is an actin-associated motor and keratin an intermediate-filament protein; actin is another filament system. The disease is multifactorial, so identifying tau does not establish that one filament defect alone explains all cases or mechanisms.
CYQ15: Structural plus/minus polarity gives microtubule tracks an orientation that can support directional organisation and motor transport. It is not a positive/negative electrical charge and does not itself synthesize ATP, RNA or protein. Motors and energy-dependent interactions provide movement; tubulin orientation supplies part of the organised track.
CYQ16: Defective keratin networks can compromise mechanical resilience and cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex with skin blistering. Tay–Sachs is a lysosomal substrate-degradation disorder, while ciliary and neurodegenerative conditions involve different mechanisms. The scenario asks for the filament/support relationship rather than suggesting every blistering presentation has this diagnosis.
CYQ17: The mitotic spindle organises chromosome alignment and segregation using microtubules, associated proteins and regulated dynamics. Lipid synthesis, glycosylation and waste digestion are not its principal cytoskeletal role. Merely retaining polymer is insufficient: controlled assembly, disassembly and movement are required for the spindle to function.
CYQ18: Paclitaxel stabilises microtubules and suppresses their normal disassembly dynamics. That can interfere with mitosis even while microtubules remain present. It does not convert tubulin into actin, destroy tubulin genes or directly define ATP synthesis. This contrasts with agents that inhibit assembly; neither mechanism implies selective effects on cancer cells alone.
CE01-Q01: Homogenisation creates a mixed preparation; separation then enriches its components before biochemical characterisation. Disruption alone does not identify a recovered organelle or prove purity. The sequence links preservation, physical separation and analytical evidence, so an assay result must be interpreted in the context of what the preparation retained.
CE01-Q02: An appropriate iso-osmotic environment helps preserve isolated organelles against osmotic injury. That goal differs from using hypotonic conditions to facilitate deliberate cell lysis. There is no single medium appropriate for every stage and target. Ask what should break and what should remain intact before treating those two uses as contradictory.
CE01-Q03: Sonication supplies high-frequency sound that creates disruptive mechanical effects including cavitation. It is not the same mechanism as pressure-driven passage through an opening or manual grinding. Heating can damage the desired material, so the lecture discusses short bursts and cooling; its volume examples are not universal instrument limits.
CE01-Q04: Mortar-and-pestle grinding is useful for relatively tough plant material, often aided by freezing in the source example. Plant walls present a different mechanical challenge from fragile membrane-bound organelles. Suitability depends on whether the goal is intact structures or soluble contents, so stronger disruption is not automatically a better preparation.
CE01-Q05: The homogenate is the suspension produced by disruption and contains a mixture of cellular components. It is not already a pure organelle preparation. Subsequent separation and assays are needed to establish enrichment, identity and retained activity. Preparation quality therefore affects the interpretation of all later fraction measurements.
CE02-Q01: The supernatant is the liquid remaining above sedimented material, while the pellet contains what collected during the spin. In differential fractionation the supernatant can supply a subsequent higher-force spin. Confusing these fractions changes what material is analysed next. Neither name independently proves the molecular identity or purity of its contents.
CE02-Q02: Differential centrifugation uses successive spins, typically applying higher forces to the transferred supernatant. Earlier and later pellets enrich different sedimenting components. The fractions are not automatically pure, because particle size, density and shape all affect sedimentation. Keep track of what was retained or transferred after each stage.
CE02-Q03: Large, relatively fast-sedimenting material such as nuclei and debris is enriched in the source's first low-force pellet. Smaller or slower-sedimenting components can remain in the supernatant for a later spin. Enrichment is conditional on the preparation and settings and is not proof that only nuclei occur in the pellet.
CE02-Q04: Relative centrifugal force depends on rotor radius as well as rotational speed. Therefore equal rpm does not guarantee equal ×g on different rotors. The lecture's example force/time conditions should not be copied as universal settings. Use the appropriate instrument specification and validated procedure rather than inferring force from speed alone.
CE02-Q05: Particles with overlapping sedimentation behaviour can co-pellet, so a differential fraction is enriched rather than completely pure. Its name identifies an intended enrichment, not conclusive composition. Marker assays, microscopy or further purification can test the claim. A larger pellet or longer spin does not by itself demonstrate a purer preparation.
CE03-Q01: Rate-zonal separation exploits different travel rates through a gradient during a controlled time interval. Size, mass and shape can create a difference even when buoyant densities are similar. Isopycnic separation instead uses equilibrium density position. Keeping those questions distinct explains why the same pair of substances may suit one method more than another.
CE03-Q02: At isopycnic equilibrium a particle bands where the surrounding medium matches its buoyant density. Size alone does not specify that position. Additional time after equilibrium is not equivalent to continued rate-zonal travel toward the bottom. An appropriate gradient must span the relevant density for the intended banding interpretation.
CE03-Q03: Rate-zonal separation relies on separated moving zones. If all material pellets, their different positions are lost and the useful separation can collapse. Isopycnic equilibrium has a different stopping principle. A longer spin is therefore not universally a better separation; its purpose and expected endpoint determine what time means.
CE03-Q04: A suitable CsCl isopycnic gradient separates nucleic acids by equilibrium buoyant density in the lecturer's example. The final band is not merely a measure of which particle initially moved fastest. Rate-zonal methods address travel-rate differences instead. State the property to be resolved before selecting the gradient method.
CE03-Q05: Marker enzymes or other appropriate assays provide evidence of organelle identity and contamination after separation. Band position alone is not a unique identity certificate. Different components can share physical properties, and collection can introduce mixing. Physical enrichment and biochemical characterisation are complementary stages of the experiment.
CE04-Q01: Preparative work aims to recover fractions for subsequent study or use. Analytical ultracentrifugation instead characterises sedimentation behaviour quantitatively. Both involve sedimentation, but producing a measurable boundary does not automatically recover pure material. The intended experimental output distinguishes the methods more clearly than the word centrifuge alone.
CE04-Q02: Analytical ultracentrifugation examines sedimentation behaviour in solution to characterise material under stated conditions. It is not simply another promise of complete purification. Interpretation depends on the model, solvent and measurement quality; the lecturer's comparison-standard wording should not be read as saying that no assumptions or instrument checks are needed.
CE04-Q03: One svedberg equals 10⁻¹³ seconds and expresses a sedimentation coefficient. It is not a unit of molecular mass. The coefficient reflects buoyancy, shape and friction as well as mass, so equal coefficients do not prove identical molecules. This is explicitly supplementary physical interpretation of the lecturer's analytical method.
CE04-Q04: Sedimentation reflects how a particle interacts with the solvent and resists motion as well as its mass. Shape-dependent friction and buoyancy therefore affect the coefficient. A heavy particle is not automatically described by mass alone in a hydrodynamic measurement. State conditions before comparing values from different preparations.
CE04-Q05: Rotor speed ratings and tube compatibility are essential equipment constraints. Choosing settings from a lecture example without checking the actual rotor/tube specifications is insufficient. This question identifies the relevant safety consideration, not a validated operating protocol or permission to run unfamiliar equipment. Instrument procedures and trained supervision remain necessary.
BI01-Q01: Spectrophotometry measures wavelength-dependent light transmission/absorption under defined conditions. A signal can support a concentration estimate in a suitable assay, but colour intensity alone does not uniquely identify an unknown substance. Wavelength selection, blanks, sample condition and calibration determine whether the numerical interpretation is appropriate.
BI01-Q02: l is the optical path length through the sample, commonly expressed in centimetres with compatible absorptivity units. ε describes molar absorptivity and c concentration. Changing path length can alter absorbance without changing concentration. The Beer–Lambert equation is explicitly supplementary context here, distinct from the source's instrument-description pages.
BI01-Q03: A blank accounts for background contribution from solvent and reagents under the chosen measurement conditions. It does not automatically remove every sample-specific interference, scattering effect or nonlinear response. Appropriate blanking is part of measurement control, not proof that the remaining absorbance uniquely identifies the intended analyte.
BI01-Q04: Absorbance is log10(I0/I), using incident intensity over transmitted intensity. If transmission is one tenth of incidence, the ratio is 10 and absorbance is 1. Reversing the ratio changes the sign and using a simple intensity difference answers another question. This equation is labelled supplementary rather than attributed as printed source text.
BI01-Q05: High concentration, scattering and interference can violate the assumptions behind a simple linear concentration estimate. A correct equation cannot repair an unsuitable sample or wavelength. Dilution and controls can test measurement behaviour when appropriate, but a blank alone is not a universal correction. Interpret the observed assay conditions before assigning a concentration.
BI02-Q01: Autoradiography maps detected emissions from radioactive label. It does not directly show every cellular structure or prove the exact chemical identity of every labelled molecule. Precursor choice, exposure, preparation and controls connect the signal to a biological interpretation. Conventional radiopaque X-ray contrast is a different mechanism.
BI02-Q02: Radiation sensitises the emulsion and development converts exposed silver halide into visible metallic silver grains. Photographic fixing removes unexposed material. Those steps are distinct from tissue fixation and from a specimen synthesising silver. The resulting pattern is detector evidence for tracer distribution, interpreted with appropriate background controls.
BI02-Q03: The direct result is a spatial distribution of radiolabel. Identifying the labelled molecules or inferring their activity requires the precursor, metabolic fate, timing and complementary controls. Label can be incorporated or redistributed, so a detected grain is not by itself a unique protein identity or proof of every biochemical process in that location.
BI02-Q04: Emission properties affect how far the signal can travel, and specimen thickness/geometry influences localisation. Exposure and preparation also matter. Merely enlarging the autoradiograph cannot recover finer biological locations than its signal permits. Distinguish where radiation was detected from an exact molecular coordinate.
BI02-Q05: Background controls help distinguish meaningful tracer signal from nonspecific or background grains, while radiation precautions address handling risk. Neither a dark grain nor a familiar specimen appearance replaces those controls. Interpretation and safe experimental conduct are separate requirements; this educational question is not an executable radioisotope procedure.
BI03-Q01: The mobile phase moves through the separation system and carries components according to their interactions. The stationary phase remains the reference phase relative to which retention occurs. A substance need not move at the solvent's full rate because it can spend time retained. The phase roles explain migration better than the final spot colour alone.
BI03-Q02: Stronger interaction with the stationary phase generally increases retention and delays elution under otherwise matched conditions. Earlier elution reflects spending relatively more time with the mobile phase, not a universal identity label. Size, charge and other properties matter through the chosen separation chemistry, so changing conditions can alter the comparison.
BI03-Q03: Partition separation depends on unequal distribution between phases, related to relative solubility under the stated conditions. Adsorption emphasizes surface interaction, and real systems can include both. Components that spend different proportions of time in the phases move differently. This mechanism is not a universal rule that every solute has one fixed migration rate.
BI03-Q04: Mobile-phase composition changes solubility and phase interactions and can therefore change retention. pH, temperature and stationary-phase chemistry can also matter. A retention comparison without matched conditions is incomplete. Choosing a solvent is part of designing the separation, not merely changing the colour of the final display.
BI03-Q05: Early elution gives retention information under the tested conditions, not a unique chemical identity. Different substances can behave similarly and conditions can alter elution. Standards and complementary evidence help interpret the result, but one coinciding retention observation alone remains insufficient proof. Physical separation and identification are related but different analytical tasks.
BI04-Q01: Keeping the baseline above the solvent allows the sample to enter the developing separation through the paper. Submerging it can wash material into the reservoir instead. A missing or faint spot after incorrect setup is not proof that the original sample lacked the analyte. Interpret the procedure before interpreting absence of signal.
BI04-Q02: Capillary action draws solvent through the paper. Components then migrate differently because of their interactions with the mobile/stationary phases. The solvent rising does not mean every sample component travels equally far or at the same rate. Distinguish movement of the developing solvent from retention of each analyte.
BI04-Q03: Mark the solvent front promptly after removing the paper because evaporation can make its location unclear. Rf needs the distance from the common origin to that front. Measuring only the highest spot or waiting for the reference to disappear can compromise the ratio. A visually neat dry chromatogram is not sufficient without its reference measurements.
BI04-Q04: Different interactions with the phases cause components to spend different proportions of time moving versus retained, producing different distances. The relationship depends on solvent and stationary-phase chemistry. Equal travel in one system does not guarantee identity, and failure to resolve two compounds does not prove that only one compound was present.
BI04-Q05: A coinciding spot position shows similar migration under the tested conditions, not definitive identity. Two substances can co-migrate in one solvent. Standards, a second separation condition and complementary evidence can improve interpretation. The result must be qualified by the system rather than treated as a universally unique fingerprint.
BI05-Q01: Rf is spot-centre travel divided by solvent-front travel, both measured from the same baseline in the same units. Using raw ruler readings can introduce an origin error, and reversing the ratio changes its meaning. Units cancel. The ratio supports conditional comparison; it does not independently identify a substance.
BI05-Q02: Measure both distances from the origin: 1.4/7.7=0.1818..., rounded to 0.18. Reversing the ratio or mixing centimetres and millimetres gives a misleading result. These are the lecturer's printed worked values, visually checked on actual p.410, rather than a claim of new pixel-exact measurements of the source illustration.
BI05-Q03: B is less strongly retained than A under the illustrated column conditions and therefore travels through and elutes earlier. This compares phase interaction; it does not prove B's unique identity or imply that B is always fastest in every solvent. Changing pH, temperature or separation chemistry can alter retention.
BI05-Q04: The printed source example gives 6.0/7.7=0.7792..., rounded to 0.78. Both measurements use the same origin and units. Rf is dimensionless, not centimetres. A matching value is useful only under matched separation conditions and is not, alone, proof that two samples are chemically identical.
BI05-Q05: The third printed worked ratio is 4.1/7.7=0.5325..., rounded to 0.53. Use the spot centre and solvent front relative to the same baseline. A ruler's zero need not be that baseline. The calculation validates the ratio from the stated distances, while identity and purity require additional evidence.
CO-Q001: A cell is the basic living structural and functional unit; an isolated DNA molecule or a virus containing genetic material is not thereby a cell. A tissue is a collection of cells, while visibility depends on the observing instrument rather than defining life. The definition describes cellular organisation: specialised cells in multicellular organisms can depend on other cells and need not reproduce independently.
CO-Q002: A cell regulates exchange across its boundary to maintain conditions for its reactions. Antibody secretion belongs to specialised immune cells, not every cell, and peptidoglycan is characteristic of many bacterial walls rather than a universal cellular product. Cells can also change shape, so maintaining one constant geometry is not a general requirement for life.
CO-Q003: Subcellular structure organises enzymes, substrates and local conditions, connecting the cell's architecture with its biochemical activity. Composition matters, but composition alone without spatial organisation does not capture that explanation; organism cell count or neighbour distance is not the lecturer's stated principle. The review distractor has been clarified because the earlier option about component organisation duplicated the meaning of the keyed answer.
CO-Q004: A unicellular organism performs major life functions within one cell, demonstrating that tissues are not required for every form of life. Responses, metabolism and reproduction can occur at the cellular level rather than being unique to multicellular organisms. This does not imply that each specialised cell isolated from a multicellular organism can survive or reproduce unaided.
CO-Q005: Antibody secretion is a specialised immune function, unlike the lecturer's general framework of compartmentalisation, regulated exchange, genetic direction and continuity of life. The review stem asks about that framework rather than claiming every specialised cell performs every function at all times. Mature mammalian erythrocytes, for example, lack a nucleus; general cellular principles must be distinguished from exceptions in differentiated cells.
CO-Q006: Functional means that organised cellular processes perform the activities on which the organism depends. Structural refers to cells as building units; the two ideas therefore complement each other. Skeletal, hormonal and circulatory describe particular systems or roles and cannot replace the general functional description for all cellular life.
CO-Q007: Cell shape can be adapted to a task, such as a long process supporting communication or a flattened form shortening an exchange path. The source also includes mechanical and physical influences; functional adaptation is not the sole determinant. Equal volume, a universal wall or a fixed cytoplasmic viscosity would incorrectly remove the variation the lesson explains.
CO-Q008: Neighbouring cells can exert forces that deform or constrain a cell, so its surroundings contribute to shape. Nuclear colour, chromosome number alone and the organism's number of organs do not describe that mechanical interaction. Membrane-cortex properties and functional adaptation also contribute; selecting this listed factor does not make shape depend on neighbours alone.
CO-Q009: The lecturer's 100-trillion figure is a historical estimate of total cells, not an exact constant shared by every person. It is neither the number of cell types nor the count in each organ. Body size, cell definitions and estimation methods affect totals, so recognising the estimate is more defensible than treating it as a precise modern biological measurement.
CO-Q010: Geometry can support a specialised task by changing exchange area, mechanical behaviour or the distance over which material must move. This links form with function without claiming that shape alone determines every activity. The nucleus is not the only influence on shape, and specialised cells need not perform identical tasks.
CO-Q011: The plasma membrane bounds an animal cell and regulates exchange with its environment. The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus, and the mitochondrial matrix is an internal organelle compartment. Animal cells do not have the external cell wall found in plants and many microbes, so wall and membrane must not be used interchangeably.
CO-Q012: Compression by adjacent cells is an application of the lecturer's mechanical-action factor: contact forces can alter the cell's outline. The question holds the other named influences similar to focus on that change. Mitochondrial number, DNA quantity and membrane colour do not directly explain the stated compression; internal cortical mechanics can influence how strongly a cell responds.
CO-Q013: A cube has six square faces. With L=2 cm, one face is L²=4 cm², so total area is 6×4=24 cm²; 8 cm³ would instead be its volume. Keep the number of faces, the squared length and the area units together rather than confusing total surface with one face or with enclosed space.
CO-Q014: Volume measures enclosed space, so V=L³=4³=64 cm³. The 16 cm² value is one face's area, while 96 cm² is the total surface area of that cube. Cubic units are part of the result: an area and a volume cannot be exchanged merely because both calculations use the same length.
CO-Q015: For L=4 cm, SA=6×4²=96 cm² and V=4³=64 cm³, giving SA/V=1.5 cm⁻¹. The equivalent formula 6/L gives the same answer. The ratio is area per volume, not volume per area, and it has inverse-length units rather than being a dimensionless count.
CO-Q016: Doubling length multiplies volume by 2³=8, whereas surface area rises by 2²=4. The factor of two applies to side length only. This difference in scaling is why a larger cube can have more absolute surface yet less surface for each unit of its internal volume.
CO-Q017: For similar cubes SA/V=6/L, so increasing L reduces the ratio. Surface area itself does not fall to zero or stop increasing; it grows more slowly than volume. Distinguishing total area from area per unit volume avoids the mistaken conclusion that a larger object necessarily has less exchange surface in absolute terms.
CO-Q018: Exchange often occurs across surface while demand relates to internal volume, so enlargement can increase demand faster than exchange capacity. Transport proteins do exist, and large cells can carry out reactions; those distractors turn a scaling constraint into false absolute prohibitions. Shape, folds, metabolic demand and internal transport can modify the constraint, which is why SA/V is an explanation rather than a universal size limit.
CO-Q019: A typical eukaryotic cell has its nuclear DNA enclosed by a nuclear envelope. Prokaryotic DNA is not enclosed in that kind of nucleus, but prokaryotes still have ribosomes and organised cellular activity. The word typical matters: some differentiated eukaryotic cells lose their nucleus, and a peptidoglycan wall is a bacterial rather than defining eukaryotic feature.
CO-Q020: Peptidoglycan is the characteristic wall polymer of most bacteria. Chitin occurs in fungal walls, cellulose in plant walls, and collagen is an extracellular animal structural protein. Most is a necessary qualification because some bacteria lack a conventional cell wall; this distinction also prevents confusing bacterial and archaeal envelopes.
CO-Q021: Both cellular groups translate RNA into protein using ribosomes. Golgi apparatus, mitochondria and nuclear envelopes are membrane-associated structures of eukaryotic organisation rather than universal features of all cells. Shared ribosomal function does not mean prokaryotic and eukaryotic ribosomes have identical composition or antibiotic sensitivity.
CO-Q022: Archaeal walls, when present, lack bacterial peptidoglycan and can use other materials. This distinguishes their chemistry from bacteria without claiming every archaeon has the same wall. A cell wall is also different from the plasma membrane: absence of a particular wall polymer does not mean absence of a cellular boundary.
CO-Q023: Some archaea have histone proteins, so the slide's blanket description of prokaryotic DNA packaging needs a domain-specific qualification. Bacteria generally use other DNA-associated proteins, and possession of histones does not create a membrane-bound nucleus. The correct answer recognises biological variation rather than replacing one universal claim with another.
CO-Q024: Cell theory includes the cellular composition of organisms, the cell as a basic unit of life, and the origin of cells from pre-existing cells. A universal membrane-bound nucleus would exclude prokaryotes, while spontaneous generation is not the theory's account of ordinary cell reproduction. The lecturer assigns cell theory on actual PDF p.201 but does not explain it there, so this explanation remains explicitly supplementary.
OR02-Q01: Glyoxysomal pathways allow carbon from seed lipid reserves to contribute to carbohydrates that support early growth. Fatty acids provide acetyl-CoA, and the glyoxylate-cycle bypass helps conserve carbon for subsequent sugar-forming pathways. Spindle formation, ribosome assembly and silica-related injury concern other structures; this plant pathway should not be assumed to occur in human cells.
OR02-Q02: The source specifically names succinate as a net glyoxylate-cycle product. Glucose is a downstream carbohydrate product of linked metabolism, not the named direct product of this cycle; lactate and urate belong to different pathways. Succinate must undergo further conversions, so the simplified slide should not be read as a one-step succinate-to-glucose reaction.
OR02-Q03: Hydrogenosomes can release molecular hydrogen, H₂, during anaerobic energy metabolism. Molecular hydrogen is distinct from oxygen, carbon dioxide, ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. The name identifies a metabolic feature of particular organelles; it does not imply that all cells growing without oxygen possess hydrogenosomes.
OR02-Q04: Hydrogenosomes occur in certain anaerobic eukaryotes, including some trichomonads, ciliates and fungi. Mature human erythrocytes do not acquire hydrogenosomes simply because they lack conventional aerobic organelles. Chloroplasts and extracellular collagen are different structures; oxygen-independent metabolism is a broader category than the presence of this organelle.
OR02-Q05: Glycosomes are listed without detailed development in this source passage, so the question tests the limit of what the slides establish. They must not be confused with glycogen granules merely because their names resemble one another. Centrosomes organise microtubules, nucleoli support ribosome biogenesis and phagosomes contain engulfed cargo; those structures are not the undeveloped microbody term requested.
OR05-Q01: The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum, connecting nuclear-envelope structure with the ER system. This does not make the nuclear interior the same compartment as the ER lumen: the perinuclear space is the lumenal continuation. Lysosomes, centriolar microtubules and the plasma membrane do not form the stated direct continuity.
OR05-Q02: Nuclear pore complexes regulate exchange across the nuclear envelope, including selective transport of many proteins and RNA-containing particles. They are not merely unrestricted holes whose diameter alone determines entry. Catalase is an enzyme, glyoxysomes are metabolic organelles and collagen is an extracellular structural protein; none provides the nucleus's selective gateway.
OR05-Q03: A typical human diploid somatic nucleus contains 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. A haploid gamete has 23; 44 counts the autosomes without the two sex chromosomes in the usual diploid complement. DNA replication doubles DNA content and sister chromatids before division, but does not automatically make the usual replicated metaphase complement 92 chromosomes when counted by centromeres.
OR05-Q04: A nucleosome packages DNA around a histone core, forming a repeating organisational unit of chromatin. Hydrogenosomes, phagosomes and peroxisomes are organelles with other functions rather than units of DNA packaging. Packaging must support regulated access as well as compaction; chromatin is not simply permanently inaccessible DNA.
OR05-Q05: Transcription uses a DNA template to synthesise RNA. Messenger RNA can subsequently guide protein synthesis, but transcription also makes RNAs that are not translated, including rRNA and tRNA. Collagen fibres, centrioles and peroxide are not direct transcription products; distinguish the information-copying process from later assembly or metabolic chemistry.
OR06-Q01: The nucleolus is a major site of rRNA production, processing and ribosomal-subunit assembly. Ribosomal proteins are made in the cytoplasm and imported to join rRNA; assembled subunits are subsequently exported. This is distinct from fatty-acid oxidation, lysosomal digestion or catalase production, and does not mean all mature translation takes place in the nucleolus.
OR06-Q02: The nucleolus has no enclosing lipid membrane, although it is a spatially organised region within the membrane-enclosed nucleus. A compartment can therefore be functionally distinct without having its own bilayer. Single and double membranes describe other organelles, while a bacterial cell wall is neither a nucleolar boundary nor part of normal nuclear architecture.
OR06-Q03: Nucleolar organiser regions contain arrays of rRNA genes around which nucleolar organisation develops. A centromere is associated with chromosome segregation and a telomere with chromosome ends; neither name alone identifies the rRNA-gene region. The nucleolus forms through organised gene activity and assembly, rather than chromosomes simply becoming one undifferentiated body.
OR06-Q04: Chromatin is DNA associated with proteins, including histones and other regulatory or structural components. It is present during interphase as well as in highly condensed mitotic chromosomes. Free RNA alone and cytoskeletal microtubules are different materials; changes in compaction alter access without turning chromatin into a different fundamental substance.
OR06-Q05: Nucleolar number and appearance can vary with cell type, activity and cell-cycle state, so a fixed number for every cell or species is not a sound universal rule. Nucleoli also reorganise during division rather than remaining unchanged. The review retains this scientific qualification instead of converting the slide's fixed-number simplification into an assessment fact.
OR07-Q01: A typical centriole contains nine peripheral microtubule triplets. Nine counts the triplet groups, not nine total individual tubules, and 9×3 is different from the 9+2 axonemal pattern of many motile cilia. Distinguish the architecture of the organising basal structure from the ciliary shaft it can help organise.
OR07-Q02: The typical paired centrioles are approximately perpendicular, forming an angle near 90°. That describes their relative axes, not the angle between each neighbouring microtubule triplet around a centriole. The approximation and cellular context matter; the centrosome also includes surrounding material that nucleates microtubules.
OR07-Q03: Animal-cell centrosomes help organise spindle microtubules for chromosome alignment and segregation. The surrounding pericentriolar material is important to nucleation; the answer should not be reduced to centrioles acting alone. Lysosomal-enzyme synthesis, GM2 breakdown and rRNA transcription belong to other pathways or compartments.
OR07-Q04: In the radial array described, minus ends lie near the organising centre and plus ends extend toward the periphery. Plus ends can grow or shrink; the label does not mean compulsory outward movement or positive electrical charge. Other cellular microtubule arrays can have different arrangements, so the question specifies the typical centrosomal case.
OR07-Q05: A centriole can become a basal body that organises a cilium's microtubules. A nucleosome packages DNA, a residual body contains incompletely digested material and a glyoxysome supports specialised plant metabolism. The basal body's triplet architecture should be distinguished from the doublets in many ciliary axonemes.
CYQ01: Microtubules are hollow tubulin-based structures with an outer diameter around 25 nm in the lecture. Intermediate filaments are approximately 10 nm and actin filaments approximately 7–8 nm, so they are narrower. The 25 nm value is an external diameter, not a length or a count of protofilaments; dimensions alone do not identify a motor protein.
CYQ02: Actin subunits assemble into microfilaments. Tubulin instead forms microtubules, keratin belongs to an intermediate-filament family and dynein is a motor associated with microtubules. Separating a polymer's building protein from a motor that travels on a filament helps explain both architecture and movement.
CYQ03: Myosin motors interact with actin and couple ATP-dependent changes to force or movement. Kinesin and dynein principally use microtubule tracks, while tau is a microtubule-associated regulatory protein rather than the actin motor requested. A filament supplies a track or force-bearing scaffold; a motor is a different component of the movement system.
CYQ04: Intermediate filaments help cells resist tensile stress and mechanical deformation. Myosin-associated contraction involves actin, while hollow tubulin tracks are microtubules that can support motor-driven cargo transport. These broad roles overlap in whole-cell mechanics, but intermediate filaments are not interchangeable with an ATP-powered motor or a microtubule transport track.
CYQ05: Kinesin, dynein and myosin are motor-protein families that convert chemical energy into movement in cytoskeletal systems. Actin, tubulin and keratin instead form major structural filaments. Tau associates with microtubules, while collagen and laminin are extracellular matrix components; being structural or protein-based does not itself make a molecule a cytoskeletal motor.
CYQ06: The lecturer lists outer diameters of about 25 nm for microtubules, 10 nm for intermediate filaments and 8 nm for actin filaments. Standard descriptions often round actin to about 7 nm, so the source-specific 8 nm value is not an exact universal measurement. Check the narrowest-to-widest order as well as the numbers; none is the filament's total length.
CYQ07: The red-cell membrane skeleton supports a flexible biconcave outline and helps it tolerate deformation during circulation. It is not a mitotic spindle, nucleolus or Golgi stack; mature mammalian red cells lack those structures. Shape and deformability depend on the membrane-skeleton system and cell conditions together, rather than a rigid internal frame holding an unchangeable shape.
CYQ08: A protofilament is a longitudinal chain of α/β-tubulin dimers. Neighbouring protofilaments associate laterally to form the hollow microtubule wall. A pore, chromosome arm or ATPase complex is a different organisational structure; a protofilament is neither the whole microtubule nor a separate membrane compartment.
CYQ09: A typical cytoplasmic microtubule wall has 13 protofilaments arranged around its circumference. Each protofilament contains many tubulin dimers along the length, so 13 is not the total subunit count. The 25 nm outer diameter and 9+2 axonemal arrangement describe different scales and must not be substituted for the protofilament number.
CYQ10: The main microtubule building unit is an α-tubulin/β-tubulin heterodimer. Actin and myosin form a different track-and-motor partnership; kinesin and dynein are motor families, while keratin and tau have different structural or associated roles. Repeated orientation of the tubulin dimers gives the resulting polymer its structural polarity.
CYQ11: Plus and minus distinguish structurally different microtubule ends created by oriented tubulin dimers. They do not identify positive and negative electrical charges or two different kinds of cell. This polarity can organise assembly and motor direction, but the labels alone do not mean one end can only grow and the other can only shrink.
CYQ12: Dynamic instability is switching between microtubule growth and shrinkage, including transitions called catastrophe and rescue. It is not DNA replication or the synthesis of motor proteins. Changes in tubulin addition and end stability permit rapid rearrangement, so a functioning cytoskeleton need not be either permanently rigid or wholly dissolved.
CYQ19: Vincristine interferes with microtubule assembly and is explicitly identified as a chemotherapy drug in the source. Paclitaxel is also an anticancer drug, but stabilises microtubules and inhibits their disassembly; the revised stem distinguishes mechanism because the earlier broad wording admitted both drugs. Tubulin is the filament building protein and kinesin a motor, not the requested chemotherapy example.
CYQ20: Spindle function requires microtubule rearrangement, so suppressing disassembly can disrupt mitosis despite retaining polymer. More DNA repair, ribosome assembly or glucose does not describe that stabilising mechanism. A static abundance of tracks is not equivalent to a functional dynamic spindle, just as inhibiting assembly is a different route to disrupting the same process.
CYQ21: Intermediate filaments are about 10 nm across, between narrower actin filaments and wider microtubules. Myosin is a motor-protein family rather than the intermediate-sized filament class. Approximate diameters support classification, but filament composition and function provide additional evidence and should be considered with size.
CYQ22: Kinesin and dynein are major microtubule-based motor families. Myosin principally uses actin; actin itself is a filament subunit, not its motor, while keratin, laminin, tau and collagen have other roles. Do not infer that every kinesin has the same direction or function merely because the family commonly associates with microtubules.
CYQ23: The cytoskeleton is a dynamic protein-filament network that supports organisation, force transmission and movement. It is neither a cell wall nor a DNA-storage organelle or a lipid layer. Dynamic does not mean unsupported or chaotic: regulated assembly, linking proteins and motors allow stability of overall cell form alongside local change.
CYQ24: Healthy cells also use microtubules for division, intracellular transport and specialised structures. A drug targeting tubulin dynamics therefore cannot be assumed to affect tumour cells alone, even if it has therapeutic benefit. Normal cells can divide, and the mechanism does not require direct removal of all DNA; benefit and adverse effects must both be distinguished from the target's basic biology.
CM_MCQ_24-84: Cytosol is the aqueous cytoplasmic phase outside membrane-enclosed organelles; cytoplasm includes that phase and cytoplasmic organelles. Nucleoplasm is inside the nucleus, chromatin is DNA with associated proteins and the glycocalyx is a carbohydrate-rich surface layer. Cytosol is not pure water: dissolved proteins, metabolites and ions give it biochemical functions.
CM_MCQ_24-85: The hydrocarbon fatty-acid tails are the principal hydrophobic regions of a typical phospholipid. The phosphate-containing head and attached polar groups interact favourably with water. Hydrophobic does not mean that a tail actively pushes water away; clustering reduces unfavourable exposure and helps explain bilayer organisation.
CM_MCQ_24-86: Phospholipids have both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, so heads face aqueous surroundings while tails cluster in the interior. Their tails do not form favourable bonds with water, and membrane proteins need not assemble first for lipids to self-organise. The bilayer still has selective permeability: self-assembly does not make it impermeable to every substance.
CM_MCQ_24-87: The fluid mosaic model describes a lipid bilayer with embedded or associated proteins and other components. Lipids and many proteins can move laterally, although cytoskeletal anchoring and domains can constrain movement. It is not a rigid protein shell, a single monolayer or pure protein; fluidity and the bilayer's barrier function coexist.
CM_MCQ_24-88: Glycogen granules are cytoplasmic carbohydrate-storage inclusions, alongside the lipid droplets mentioned in the source. Nuclear pores belong to the nuclear envelope, cristae are inner mitochondrial membrane folds and centrioles organise microtubule-related structures. Recognising an inclusion does not make it a membrane-enclosed organelle or a glycosome.
CM_MCQ_24-89: The plasma membrane forms the cell's boundary with the external environment and helps regulate exchange. A nucleolus supports ribosome biogenesis, a centrosome organises microtubules and a ribosome translates RNA. Internal membrane-bound organelles have their own boundaries, but those do not replace the plasma membrane as the boundary of the whole cell.
CM_MCQ_24-96: A transmembrane protein crosses the lipid bilayer, with membrane-facing hydrophobic regions and portions exposed to water. Peripheral proteins associate at a surface or through other proteins, while soluble cytosolic and nucleolar proteins do not necessarily enter a membrane. All transmembrane proteins are integral, but an integral protein need not span the entire bilayer.
CM_MCQ_24-97: The glycocalyx contains carbohydrate chains attached to membrane proteins and lipids at the external cell surface. It supports recognition and surface interactions rather than forming a cytoplasmic microtubule network. Nucleoli and centrosomes are internal structures; the location and carbohydrate-rich composition together identify the correct answer.
CM_MCQ_24-98: Peripheral proteins associate with a membrane surface or another membrane protein without spanning the hydrophobic core. They can have structural, enzymatic or signalling functions, so they are not all ion channels or pure lipids. Relatively loose is a comparison of association type, not a guarantee that every peripheral protein detaches easily under physiological conditions.
CM_MCQ_24-99: A receptor recognises a signal and initiates or participates in a cellular response. Binding alone is insufficient to define every binding protein as a receptor: carriers bind transported solutes, for example. Phospholipids, glycogen and cholesterol have other structural or storage roles and are not the protein type requested.
CM_MCQ_24-100: A carrier transporter binds its solute and changes conformation during movement across the membrane. A structural anchor, a receptor acting only in signal transduction and an enzyme that does not transport cargo do not perform that stated task. Carrier-mediated transport can be passive or energy-coupled, so conformational change alone does not establish active transport.
CM_MCQ_24-101: Plasma-membrane glycolipid carbohydrate groups generally face the extracellular space, contributing to the external glycocalyx. Their polar sugars are not normally buried in the hydrophobic core or restricted to the cytosolic face. This asymmetry matters for recognition: a diagram should distinguish the two membrane faces instead of depicting identical sugar exposure on both sides.
